answer:
**A hybrid combines compact recurrent memory with occasional explicit access to past tokens.** State-space layers summarize history into a fixed-size state. Attention layers keep token-level keys and values and can retrieve specific prior content directly. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21060)

If one of eight otherwise comparable layers uses conventional attention, that attention-cache portion is roughly one eighth of an all-attention stack. However, recurrent states, other buffers, head counts, and widths still contribute to total memory.

**One attention layer can help retrieval without guaranteeing every long-context task.** Needle lookup tests recovery of a particular fact under a particular setup. Distractors, multiple facts, reasoning chains, and changing positions may expose different limitations.

A 7:1 ratio is therefore an architectural choice to test, not a formula for near-perfect recall or exactly eightfold total-memory savings. Compare complete task quality, total serving memory, latency, and sustained context behavior. The goal is a useful quality–efficiency tradeoff, not preserving one benchmark score while overlooking other capabilities.

**Technical details and references.**

A hybrid keeps recurrent/linear-state layers for efficient long-context processing and selected full-attention layers for explicit content-based retrieval from previous tokens. If only one of eight otherwise comparable layers stores a conventional attention KV cache, that portion of cache storage is roughly one eighth of an all-attention model. Recurrent state and architecture-specific buffers still consume memory. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21060)

Almost-perfect needle retrieval is an empirical benchmark result under specific architectures and training, not guaranteed by a 7:1 ratio. Needle placement, distractors, multi-hop reasoning, context length, and precision affect performance. Compare full-task quality and total serving memory/latency, including attention head counts and state sizes. A single successful synthetic retrieval benchmark does not establish equivalent long-context reasoning or an exact eightfold reduction in all memory.
